text: Write it down the moment it shows up. An open loop on paper stops nagging.
A concrete plan for a task removes its intrusion into other work — you do not need to finish it, only to decide when.
Keep Today tiny. Three to five items you will actually finish beat twelve you will carry over.
Your estimate is optimistic — everyone's is. That is why every estimate is shown padded.
Plan only the next step, not the whole project. The master list keeps the rest safe.
practice: Separate the backlog from the daily commitment

text: Give a task a time and a place (`@9`, `when I sit at the desk`) and it is far more likely to happen.
Decide tonight what tomorrow starts with. The morning then has no decision to make.
Estimates above 90 minutes hide several tasks. Split them and each part gets a real chance.
A calendar has capacity; a list does not. If it does not fit between the anchors, it does not fit.
Leave one to two hours of slack. The day always brings something you did not plan.
Over capacity? Move one item to tomorrow now, while it is a choice and not a slip.
Fixed anchors, flexible content: the lecture does not move, the reading does.
Halfway through a long block, check: on track? An intermediate deadline works better than a final one.
One block slipped? Move only the next one. Re-planning the whole day is how days get lost.
Skipped. One miss changes nothing; the next block is what counts.
Being kind to yourself after a slip predicts less procrastination next time, not more.
Press `.` for a fresh start: the afternoon, tomorrow or Monday is a clean slate. Use it.
Two minutes on the task beats twenty minutes of planning it. Press `2` and begin.
A fallback decided in advance ("15 minutes at 16:00") turns a missed block into a smaller win.
Never miss twice. One miss is noise; two starts a new pattern.
Missing one day did not hurt the habit. The two-minute version today keeps the chain intact.
practice: Missing once does not break a habit

text: "5 of the last 7" is the honest number. Streaks reset to zero; consistency does not.
Attach the habit to something that already happens: right after breakfast, right after the last lecture.
Rescheduled three times? Either drop it or make it tiny. Carrying it costs more than deciding.
Small wins, visible every day, are the strongest driver of a good working week.
A weekly review is where the backlog gets honest: what still matters, what never will.
